transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20 17:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Mark Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Blake (Helio CTO), Marta Lopez (Infra Lead), Samir Khan (Security), Elena Rossi (ML Eng)

Summary: quick intro then dove into capacity numbers, isolation needs, burst policy and lots of back-and-forth on failover/regions. Several references to security controls and potential private deployment.

[00:00] Mark Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Mark from Redwood here, with Priya the SE. Quick agenda - sizing, isolation needs, burst/fallbacks, and next steps.
[00:18] Jordan Blake (Helio CTO): Thanks Mark. Quick context — we're building a real-time recommendation and search reranking layer for our consumer product. Latency matters a lot, especially 95th P for generation for user-facing flows. We're exploring reserved GPUs to get predictable performance.
[00:34] Priya Patel (Redwood SE): Got it. Can you give a sense of QPS and sequence lengths? Even ballpark helps us decide GPU class and headroom.
[00:46] Elena Rossi (ML Eng): Typical request is 1.6 requests/sec per model instance at peak per user session, but bursty — sometimes spike to ~250 concurrent requests across region. Sequence length average is 120 tokens in, 80 tokens out.
[01:05] Marta Lopez (Infra Lead): And we run in us-east-1 primarily; might expand to eu-west later. Data residency is a checkbox for EU customers. Also we need VPC isolation; on-prem is on the table but later stage.
[01:22] Priya: Cool. For that traffic profile, our initial back-of-envelope is that you'd want a pool in the 8-16 GPU range to cover baseline with room for burst, depending on model size and quantization. Can I ask what model families you're evaluating?
[01:36] Jordan: Mostly open Llama-like variants and a couple of 70B dense models. We are keen on 8-bit quantized for cost.
[01:44] Mark: Okay, so quantization plus batching strategy will drive throughput. Quick note: Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools with configurable burst + region failover. We'll propose a config that keeps baseline reserved and allows bursts to use either reserved spare capacity or a lower-tier pool with fallbacks.
[02:05] Samir Khan (Security): On the security side, we need KMS integration, customer-managed keys, RBAC that maps to our SSO via SAML, and full audit logs for inference traffic. Is that all available with Dedicated?
[02:18] Mark: Yes — Redwood Dedicated supports customer KMS, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logging. We also have a private deployment option if you need an air-gapped setup; some of our customers take that for strict compliance.
[02:33] Samir: Great. Also HIPAA is in scope for some of our enterprise customers; will need SOC2 Type 2 evidence.
[02:41] Priya: We can share our SOC2 report and a HIPAA checklist. We'll set a security deep-dive with our compliance team next week.
[02:50] Jordan: Can you walk through how burst works? We don't want failures when we're seeing big spikes around events.
[02:57] Priya: Sure. The model is: you reserve a baseline pool sized for steady state. Then you configure burst rules — e.g., ephemeral scale up to N additional GPUs (either warm spare or on-demand) with limits. We also support routing policy to fall back to cheaper model variants or a hosted fallback if dedicated capacity is saturated. There's also prefix caching for repeated prompts which reduces token work.
[03:24] Marta: How long does it take to scale up GPUs for burst? We care about tail latency during scale.
[03:30] Priya: If you use warm spare GPUs (pre-warmed instances), scale is sub-2s to start serving. If you rely on cold on-demand provisioning, it could be 60-180s. That's why we recommend a small always-on warm buffer for predictable tails.
[03:48] Jordan: Ok, so cost tradeoff — warm spares cost more but protect latency. What about pre-warming model weights and KV cache behavior?
[03:56] Priya: Right — we support KV cache warm-up and pre-loaded models. There is an operational runbook to snapshot/generate model cache states. For large context models, warming KV cache on warm spares can shave off 50-200ms. We'll include cache pre-warm scripts in the benchmark package.
[04:12] Elena: Quick clarifying, when you say KV cache are you referring to the user session key-value cache? We've seen some vendors call that K V cache, k-v, K-B, transcription sometimes messes it up.
[04:24] Mark: Yep K-V cache — it'll store past tokens to speed autoregeneration.
[04:28] Marta: What about multi-tenant isolation? We need node-level isolation for certain customers.
[04:34] Priya: Dedicated supports node isolation and per-tenant pools. For strict isolation we can allocate GPUs into a private pool per tenancy. There's also network-level VPC peering or private link.
[04:45] Samir: Do audit logs include token-level metadata or just request metadata? We can't store full PII in logs.
[04:51] Mark: By default audit logs include request metadata (timestamps, model id, route id, latency). We redact or don't store full inputs unless you opt-in for debug mode. We also support token redaction and configurable retention.
[05:07] Jordan: Can we do a small pilot to validate 95th P latency and cost per 1M tokens?
[05:12] Mark: Yes. Priya will send a benchmark script and a sample dataset. We'll run an initial calibration with one model on 4 GPUs and then propose scaling.
[05:22] Priya: I'll include scripts for both steady-state load and event-surge load (sustained for 10 minutes). We'll ask for your test keys and a minimal dataset.
[05:31] Marta: On routing — if dedicated pool is saturated and fallback to hosted happens, what happens to data plane? We need to ensure data doesn't leave VPC.
[05:39] Priya: Good callout. By default a fallback to Redwood hosted would route out of your VPC. If data residency or egress is not allowed, we can instead route to a lower-cost variant within your private pool or queue requests. For strict compliance, you'd usually want a private deployment or to size for enough headroom.
[05:58] Samir: About metrics and observability — we need per-route SLO dashboards, tracing to correlate requests, and token-level cost attribution.
[06:08] Mark: That's all supported in Redwood Console. You can get token breakdowns per route, per-model, and per-token-type. We'll show a demo during the pilot.
[06:17] Jordan: Heart of the matter: give me an example config you'd recommend for our traffic — we said 250 concurrent at spikes, avg seq 120/80.
[06:25] Priya: Roughly, assuming a 70B quan-tized model on A100-style GPUs, 8 GPUs as baseline with a 4-GPU warm spare pool for bursts would handle a lot of cases. If you want 95th P under 300ms reliably at peak, increase warm spares to 6 GPUs. Exact numbers depend on batch sizes and whether you accept a small increase in latency for lower cost.
[06:52] Elena: Could we run a canary where 10% traffic goes to a fallback hosted model during surges to see user impact?
[06:59] Mark: Absolutely — canary routing and A/B is supported via rollout policies. We can also automate fallback rules based on latency or error thresholds.
[07:08] Jordan: Any minimum commitments or contract terms for Dedicated?
[07:12] Mark: Dedicated is reserved monthly or annual commits. We can do a short pilot-month with a lower commit to start, but for price efficiency longer commitments are recommended. We'll include a flexible burst allowance in the proposal.
[07:25] Marta: Ops — who owns incident runbooks? If a GPU pool degrades, what's the operational flow?
[07:33] Priya: We'll provide per-customer runbooks: automatic retry policies, routing to regional failover, alerts to your PagerDuty (if you want), and Redwood on-call escalation. Customers own their app-level retry semantics; Redwood manages infra-level failover.
[07:50] Samir: For encryption at rest and in transit, do you support customer-managed HSM or only KMS?
[07:56] Mark: We support KMS integrations and in some private installs we can integrate with HSMs. We'll capture your specific encryption requirements in the security deep-dive.
[08:06] Jordan: Any hidden costs we should know about? E.g., egress, KMS requests, cold start penalties?
[08:12] Mark: Main costs are reserved GPU-hours, ephemeral burst GPU-hours, tokens served, and storage for model artifacts. KMS requests are usually small but we'll itemize them. Egress is cloud provider egress if you cross regions. We'll call out cold-start warm-up cost separately.
[08:29] Elena: For the benchmark, can we instrument our client to send user-like requests (temperature, top-p) to mimic production?
[08:35] Priya: Yes. We'll give a template that covers top-p, temp, max tokens, stop sequences. Also we'll log latencies and tail percentiles.
[08:44] Jordan: Ok, let's talk timeline. We want a pilot in early March and a decision by late March if the numbers are good.
[08:51] Mark: That fits our standard cadence. We'll target benchmarks this week, pilot next week.
[08:57] Marta: Small point — we need SAML metadata and SSO test account as part of pilot.
[09:02] Mark: We'll include SSO setup steps in the runbook.
[09:07] Samir: I'll follow up with a list of compliance questions — retention windows, redaction options, and if we can get a mutual NDA addendum for HIPAA specifics.
[09:15] Mark: Sounds good. We'll route the security deep-dive to Priya and our compliance lead.
[09:21] Elena: One last technical nit — how do you handle model rollouts? We need canary + automatic rollback if generation quality drops.
[09:29] Priya: Redwood supports pinned versions, canaries, A/B routing, and automatic fallback to previous stable model on error threshold. We also support quality monitoring tied to prompt eval sets so you can track regressions.
[09:42] Jordan: Great. Any blockers from Redwood side for doing a 2-week pilot?
[09:47] Mark: No blockers. We'll need your traffic samples, a test key, and SSO test creds. We'll prepare the dedicated capacity proposal by Tuesday.
[09:56] Jordan: Good. Thanks all.
[09:59] Mark: Recap: Redwood to send pricing + architecture, Priya to share benchmark scripts, Samir to share security Qs, Marta to provide traffic CSV, schedule security deep-dive and pilot kickoff.
[10:15] Jordan: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
questions: What is the warm spare GPU recommendation for our 250-concurrent spikes?
How is KV cache pre-warm handled and how much latency does it save?
If private deployment is required, what is the timeline and contract difference vs Dedicated?
notes: Customer leaning toward Dedicated initially with a possible Private deployment later for EU data residency
Priority is predictable 95th percentile latency during event surges
Security team requested SOC2, HIPAA checklist and SAML/KMS details
